hypothesis: Among truly oceanic islands and archipelagos (never joined to a continent), nearly all have at least one native bat species, and a large share of the remote ones have a bat species found nowhere else.
pass_criterion: Take a list of oceanic islands or archipelagos with land area ≥500 km² that were never connected to a continent. Fix the list from a geological source before looking at the range data. Using PHYLACINE 1.2 present-natural range rasters for Chiroptera (excluding introduced and extinct-only species), PASS if both hold: (a) at least 80% of the listed units have ≥1 native bat species; and (b) among the units with bats, at least 50% have ≥1 bat species whose entire natural range lies within that unit.
fail_criterion: FAIL if fewer than 60% of the listed oceanic units have any native bat species, or if fewer than 25% of the units with bats have an endemic bat species. Results between these bounds (60–80% for (a), or 25–50% for (b)) are reported as inconclusive and not as support.
interpretation: 'Oceanic islands' means islands of volcanic or coral origin that were never joined to a continent, for example Hawaii, Galápagos, Azores, Canaries, Madeira, Cape Verde, Mascarenes, Comoros, Fiji, Samoa, Tonga, Society Islands, Marquesas and Bonin. Continental-shelf islands are excluded. 'Ærial mammals' means Chiroptera. 'Almost every island' is operationalised as ≥80% of the listed units. 'Endemic' means the species' natural range lies only within that island or archipelago. The 'Present natural' range maps remove human-caused extinctions and introductions, so they match Darwin's natural-range sense. Modern reinterpretation: the grid is coarse (about 96.5 km cells), so only larger islands are tested. Oceanic islands with no bats, such as St Helena and Tristan da Cunha, count against the rule and are not excluded.

dataset.name: Data from: PHYLACINE 1.2: The Phylogenetic Atlas of Mammal Macroecology
dataset.publisher: Dryad (Faurby et al.; data paper in Ecology)
dataset.why_it_fits: It provides per-species 'Present natural' range rasters for all mammals, including bats, and a trait table with the Order field to select Chiroptera. Overlaying the rasters with the island list gives bat presence and endemism per island unit. The IUCN status field can check for extinct-only species.
